items.title: Customer Support Analysts, UX Researchers, and Directors of Storytelling: A Systematic Analysis of Job Advertisements for Anthropologists
items.affiliation: University of Wyoming; Wayne State University

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Anthropology graduates increasingly enter public and private practicing jobs. A decade ago, Brondo and Bennett argued that a disciplinary sea change was in motion that acknowledged applied work. Despite this recognition, the anthropological canon does not always address applied career tracks, and practicing work still encounters disciplinary stigma. Given the steep decline of academic jobs, however, we face a critical juncture, requiring a revisitation of the value of anthropological ways of knowing to careers outside the academy. To better understand how anthropological training fits into the job market, this paper presents findings from a systematic analysis of more than 300 nonacademic job advertisements directed at anthropology graduates of all levels. Results show that job ads for anthropologists include preferred technical, qualitative, and quantitative skills, yet also that epistemological approaches unique to anthropology, such as ethnographic research design and data collection and the ability to problem‐solve and translate results, are paramount. Based on these findings, we argue that anthropological training is highly valued in the practicing job market. A better understanding of nonacademic, practicing jobs for anthropologists, how to train students for these jobs, and how employers make hiring decisions deserves our attention as we consider the future relevance of anthropology.

items.title: Land, Gendered Labor, and Empire‐Making in Central Sudan

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This article offers an ethnographic analysis of Gulf Arab empire‐making in central Sudan, focusing on an Emirati‐owned farm in the Gezira region as a key site of capitalist extraction and imperial ambition. Through three overlapping vantage points—farm, port, and body—it explores how Emirati investments in Sudanese land, infrastructure, and labor reflect an emergent imperial formation that is ideological, racialized, and gendered. Drawing on multiscalar methodologies, it reveals how processes of concealment, control, and coercion operate across spatial and intimate domains, facilitated by domestic elites and obscured by discourses of Muslim solidarity and development. The article argues that examining emergent imperial formations through ethnography—formations that are continuously unsettled by different forms of resistance—allows us to better recognize sub‐imperial and imperial power in its increasingly diffuse and concealed forms, while deepening our understanding of the organizing and collective practices that threaten to destabilize this power.

items.title: Beyond the Dichotomy of Success and Failure: Making Activism Meaningful in South Korea and France

We suggest that this dichotomy, unintentionally reinforced by anthropological scholarship, has a broader analytical implication: It prevents ethnographers from seeing both goal‐oriented and prefigurative practices as equally constitutive of any form of activism. items.title: Four Questions for Ethnographers Under Trumpian Authoritarianism

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This article examines evolving challenges and ethical dilemmas facing ethnographers working under intensifying authoritarianism in the United States. Because very little of what the United States is experiencing is new, my work here is primarily curatorial in nature, drawing upon the lessons offered by scholars across disciplines in the United States and beyond for whom ethnographic research in authoritarian contexts has always been the norm. Following my recent decision to withdraw a manuscript from publication due to potential repercussions to activist interlocutors, I outline four questions for U.S.‐based ethnographers navigating heightened surveillance, repression, and vulnerability to state violence. These questions focus on (1) how to listen differently in the field and make sense of silence amid eroding public trust, (2) how to look differently and use ethnography to refuse authoritarian chrononormalization of violence, (3) how to question one's own assumptions that exposure via research and publication will necessarily lead to change, and conversely (4) how unexamined refusal to publish may constitute acquiescence in advance. Through this work, I invite scholars to engage in a disciplined hesitation as we rethink the stakes, strategies, and limits of ethnographic work in this political moment.

items.title: The Anthropocene and the End of Nuclear Disaster: Normalizing the Fukushima Nuclear Accident

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This article places the concept of disaster in critical dialogue with that of the Anthropocene, which introduces new imaginaries that negatively affect the governance of crises like nuclear accidents. I argue that tropes surrounding the Anthropocene can depict certain events as apocalyptic calamities while also portraying other events as mere “incidents” that do not warrant such labeling. I explore how specific narratives around the Anthropocene legitimize some forms of environmental harm as more important than other threats. This process creates a hierarchization of catastrophes and normalizes certain hazards as less important than others. More specifically, I claim that the very concept of a nuclear catastrophe is at risk of “disappearing” within the Anthropocene. Using ethnographic data based on the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster, which happened in Japan, I focus on three popular tropes associated with the Anthropocene that normalize the consequences of nuclear accidents: the figure of the global threat, the disappearance of the idea of pristine nature, and the promotion of resilience and adaptation to new realities. I conclude by reflecting on the broader implications of how Anthropocene discourse shapes which disasters matter and which are relegated to the status of distant, forgettable accidents.

items.title: How Anthropology Can Harm Students During a Genocide
items.affiliation: University of Toronto; University of Toronto Scarborough

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This essay is about the harm that is committed in the name of care. More specifically, it is about student requests for support during the ongoing genocide in Palestine and an anthropology department's use and weaponization of the language of “care” to do the exact opposite: to cause harm. I examine how the language of care for students and the exception of Palestine are weaponized by administrators—including anthropologists—to silence and shut down conversations about, and support for, Palestine. I demonstrate how the “permission to narrate” stems from certain methods of attention that speak to the university's alignment with settler colonialism, neoliberal capitalism, and anti‐Palestinian racism, even as the university officially acknowledges settler land relations and shares statements about “Diversity, Equity, Inclusion” (DEI). Indeed, such acts of care are often based on the condition that settler‐colonial and capitalist relations remain unchanged—that colonial whiteness remains unchanged—and any attempts to unsettle these liberal, institutional‐settler relations will be met with purposeful occlusion and harm.

items.title: Burying Futures: Artisanal Mining Deaths and the Politics of Negligence in Zimbabwe

extra.summary: ABSTRACT In the gold‐mining town of Kwekwe, central Zimbabwe, injury and death are a constant presence. Collapsing shafts, sudden explosions, gang fights, and neglected health infrastructure characterize the everyday lives of the town's impoverished residents. This article, based on ethnographic research conducted between 2019 and 2023 in Zimbabwe's artisanal and small‐scale mining regions, examines how young miners, their families, and township communities navigate a landscape where untimely deaths and near misses shape political subjectivity and reveal broader modes of state power. By examining how the state and its local enforcers respond to devastation in impoverished communities—and how these communities endure and interpret such recurring losses—the article shows that negligence is not just an absence but an active political repertoire. It contributes to anthropological debates on crisis, necropolitics, and state sovereignty in mineral‐extraction frontiers by showing how authority persists less through outright domination than through calibrated neglect: a mode of rule in which timely intervention is withheld, and the state reemerges selectively during moments of injury, death, or mourning to absorb loss as a political occasion.

items.title: Criminalizing hate speech in the Balkans

extra.summary: Abstract When does speech lose its legal protection and become criminally sanctionable because it causes violence? Among legal scholars, this is known as the “threshold problem,” and in international criminal law (ICL), the threshold is defined according to recent speech‐crime trials at the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. Yet, as borne out in ethnographic interview data, survivors and former combatants of the Yugoslav Wars disagree with ICL's approach to speech crimes. Judges in international tribunals deploy what I call endgame analysis , in which they consider the threshold of violent speech only at the inflection point when violence immediately and directly follows speech. In contrast, survivors and combatants assert that atrocity crimes resulted in part from the longer‐term accumulation of ethnic slurs and wartime misinformation enunciated by political and cultural authorities, both before and during the Yugoslav Wars. Challenging recent jurisprudence, they call for these former authorities to be held accountable for the violent, cumulative effect of their speech.

items.title: Contemplative radicals

extra.summary: Abstract Engaged Dharma Israel (EDI), a radical‐left group, combines Buddhist‐inspired contemplation with anti‐occupation activism in solidarity with Palestinians. For EDI, ethical self‐cultivation and political resistance are mutually sustaining commitments, yet their relationship demands ongoing, sometimes anxious work. Participants challenge both dharma practitioners who pursue self‐fashioning without political engagement and radical‐left activists who pursue political opposition without systematic ethical reflection, insisting each orientation is incomplete without the other. Nimrod, an everyday exemplar of EDI's approach, realizes its plural, sometimes conflicting values. Navigating risks of complicity, hostility, burnout, and physical harm, he demonstrates how participants work out the relationship between self‐cultivation and resistance, holding their respective values in productive tension and transforming them into embodied virtues. Tracing this navigation offers a generative response to a recurring anthropological question—how to analytically relate the ethical and the political—by ethnographically comparing the ways people connect, separate, or sequence them beyond any single theoretical configuration.

items.title: What about Beauvoir? Simone de Beauvoir in and for anthropology

extra.summary: While Simone de Beauvoir's distinct philosophical contributions have been considerably revisited over the last 30 years, anthropology has yet to fully engage the significance of her work. Drawing on The Ethics of Ambiguity and The Second Sex , this article argues that Beauvoir's philosophy is a critical recourse for anthropological inquiry, particularly for feminist and phenomenological approaches. I begin by situating the reader in her original philosophical method and theory, which are not simply deconstructions of gendered subjectivity, but rather profound considerations of the political, historical, social, and cultural moorings of lived experience, embodiment, and world-making, particularly for those who have been Othered . I bring further attention to her theory of ethics, which has been overlooked within anthropology, yet serves as an excellent implement for examining situated subjectivity and the temporality of ethics. After exploring three reasons potentially explicating her underuse, I detail her influence across feminist and phenomenological traditions within anthropology to demonstrate where she has been engaged both explicitly and, all the more so, implicitly. I close by suggesting that Beauvoir's theories are increasingly noticeable across anthropology, and reason that her work can serve as a praxis of intersectional philosophy that can expand conversations of diversity, ethical life, and the possibilities of freedom among oppression.

items.title: Hominin dispersals: causes, conditions, and outcomes
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: The ‘Out of Africa’ model that has dominated palaeoanthropology for nearly three decades was originally based on five elements: a recent ancestry to human populations; an African origin for the ancestral population; limited or no gene flow among archaic hominins and no admixture between modern humans and Neanderthals; a marked difference between the behaviour of modern humans and archaic populations; and a major role for dispersals. The first four of these have been significantly modified by accumulating fossil, genomic, and archaeological data. Dispersals, however, have remained central to the model, and have been extended to earlier phases of the evolution of Homo . Here we consider the evidence for dispersals in Pleistocene hominin evolution, and place these into the broader context of comparative evolutionary biology. We distinguish between dispersals that are essentially habitat tracking as climate or environment changes, and those conditioned by adaptive changes. Finally, we consider the consequences of dispersals for the structure of hominin populations, emphasizing the multiple potential outcomes of dispersals, the role of density dependence in structuring rates of divergence, and the role of centre‐edge models in understanding hominin diversity.

items.title: Equal before time: on the sensory suspension of accumulated time in Sichuan, China
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: Food and alcohol indulgence, along with tea‐drinking, gambling, and gossip, are integral to a characteristically Sichuanese ethos of ‘life enjoyment’ ( xiangshou shenghuo ). Beyond mere pleasure, sensory, ludic, and comic experiences temporarily strip participants of both their formal and subjective qualities. At the heart of this ethos thus lies a mode of relationality I understand as ‘pure sociability’ (Simmel). In pure sociability, mutual recognition and presentism intertwine: the senses are brought in sync not just for their somatic impact but as time‐space compressors that can make subjects feel fully relatable and thus realized. In redefining personhood to a baseline of sensorial experience, self and other reshape their relationship to time and to affluence, and subtly evade state‐backed imperatives of accumulated distinction. I suggest that the prominence of pure sociability in Sichuan has much to do with forging society anew over the recent three centuries in an emptied land of agricultural abundance where solidified claims to regional belonging or cultural exclusivity were largely absent. Conceptually, I aim to uncouple the problem of superfluous time from the logics of both linearity and homogenized identity, and instead foreground the human propensity for play as a possible foundation to both selfhood and temporal existence.

items.title: Staging friendship: towards an anthropology of everyday geopolitics in South Asia
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: This article studies Indian‐Bangladeshi friendship ethnographically, as a contested political imaginary, claim, and relation, from the vantage of its shared borderlands. Staging friendship, I show, is a geopolitical project that engages equally the highest echelons of the Indian and Bangladeshi states and ordinary residents of its marginalized borderlands. In conversation with the anthropological and interdisciplinary scholarship on friendship and the political aesthetics of nationalism, I develop an ethnographic frame to study friendship in and as geopolitics. Zooming in on friendship as political aesthetic and ethical practice allows us to grapple with the hegemonies and hierarchies, the elasticity and the power of such histories, and the everyday practices that constitute the geopolitical as a lively horizon. Moving beyond a traditional conception of geopolitics, this article is an invitation to imagine instead a geopolitics of friendship that centres and takes seriously the difficult work of living solidarity through differences, that many communities are not only engaged in, not as occasional, but as everyday acts of making a liveable world.

items.title: Mandala logic: mytho‐praxis as vernacular political theory in Myanmar

extra.summary: This article argues that myth‐making is a form of vernacular social theory, a way of producing conceptual arguments about how social formations work and what is at stake in them. I focus on a myth from Myanmar, the Myth of the Tea Seeds, and its attendant ritual complex, which culminates in an annual religious festival in the highland town of Namhsan. What emerges is a picture of core‐periphery politics that looks less like a dialectic of coercion and evasion, and more like a system of antagonistic mutual dependence. Here, mythology is contested ground, a site for interrogating the relationship between abstract social theorization and lived social relations amidst long local histories of accommodation and struggle.

items.title: False kings and imagined protestants: why schismogenesis does not explain variation in inequality among Indigenous societies of the Pacific Coast
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute
items.affiliation: University of Washington; University of California, Santa Barbara

extra.summary: Indigenous societies along the temperate Pacific coast of North America embody diverse cultural institutions. This variation is conventionally classified into two distinct cultural areas: the Northwest Coast (NWC) and California (CAL). Discussion of the environmental, material, social, and ideological variation in these societies has a long and continuing history in anthropology. In the last few years, two divergent accounts of this variation have appeared. One, proposed by Wengrow and Graeber, drawing on the concept of schismogenesis – ‘progressive differentiation’ at points of culture contact – posits a sharp contrast between Northwest Coast ‘Fisher‐kings’ and Californian ‘Protestant foragers’. The second views variation across the region as more continuous, focusing on how differential resource control and patron‐client dynamics can generate asymmetries in wealth and power. Our review of Wengrow and Graeber's proposal identifies several flaws: it portrays NWC culture in an over‐simplified and reductive manner, exaggerates the differences between CAL and NWC societies (particularly in the boundary region), and fails to provide convincing evidence that those differences result from oppositional differentiation (schismogenesis). We then explain why we believe opportunities for resource control offer a more empirically valid and theoretically coherent explanation for variation in political economy across these two culture areas.

items.title: A View from the Italian Side: Transit Migrants from the Soviet Union in Italy during the 1970s and 1980s

extra.summary: Abstract During the 1970s and 1980s, thousands of migrants from the Soviet Union transited through Italian territory. Awaiting Western immigrant visas, people spent weeks or months in the maritime periphery of Rome. Based on Italian archival evidence, the article discusses how this migration was perceived in Italy. The article interprets the ex-Soviet transit as an integral part of the broader migrations that crossed Europe during the second half of the twentieth century. Within the Italian context, I inscribe the transit in the tectonic shift from emigration to immigration that Italy underwent from the 1970s onward. Scholars have commented on how slowly Italian government policies and legislation came to appreciate the country’s changing migration landscape. This article goes further by connecting high-level politics to the situation on the ground—in the localities where people from the Soviet Union stayed—and shows how ordinary Italians confronted the new migratory reality face to face. Although the former Soviet citizens were transit migrants rather than immigrants proper, the challenges they faced had much in common with those encountered by many immigrants from other countries. In that sense, the reception of the ex-Soviets not only revealed the extent to which Italian society was (un)prepared for these new population dynamics but also offered an instructive preview of the larger, more bitterly contested migrations that awaited Italy and the rest of the Western world.

extra.summary: Abstract This article places maritime violence at the center of the history of international ordering. It views the transformation of the nineteenth-century Atlantic from the deck of one ship, a Baltimore-built privateer called the Irresistible. The ship’s captain seized Spanish and Portuguese shipping under a privateering commission from the Oriental Republic. Sponsorship of privateers by the Oriental Republic and other new Latin American governments reflected an open-ended Atlantic constitutionalism that recognized sovereignty at multiple scales. That constitutional context formed the background to three cases involving the Irresistible and its crew that reached the U.S. Supreme Court. The cases show how privateering politics opened to wide-ranging debates about the definition of states, war, and piracy, while preserving the indeterminacies of sovereignty in the new Atlantic system. That system, closing as it formed, was composed of new states pressured to align with powerful empires. Privateering disputes featured sharpening rhetoric about piracy as a crime under the law of nations while at the same time preserving a regime that protected low-level maritime violence. Situating the politics of piracy at the nexus of domestic and international orders, the article highlights the political uses and legal limits of the discourse of pirates as enemies of all and connects this history to an understanding of terrorism and states in the international order.

extra.summary: Abstract This article revisits the debate on the relationship between capitalism and abolition from the perspective of South Asia. It argues that bringing the antislavery debate into conversation with the extensive literature on caste opens up new comparative possibilities. Commercial slavery in the early modern Indian Ocean world is now well established, but global histories of slavery have rarely inspired global histories of antislavery. The dominant interpretation of abolition in South Asia remains focused on the contingent requirements of colonial governance. Through an analysis of legal conflicts over the status of slavery in the eastern Indian province of Bengal in the 1820s and 1830s, I argue that this approach obscures the ethical-political significance of abolition in a context shaped by caste and agrarian slavery. The emancipatory potential of abolition, however, was undermined by a colonial state committed to revenue extraction and social order, as well as by the global capitalist context of counter-revolution. By situating the colonial archive within this wider historical conjuncture, the essay shows how both the possibilities and limits of abolition emerged from the contradictions of liberalism and global capitalism. It thereby puts the South Asian case in conversation with broader histories of revolution and counter-revolution.

extra.summary: This brief essay memorializes Johannes Fabian and his contribution to Critique of Anthropology by reviewing his contribution to the journal and his conception of critique in anthropology. It highlights not just Fabian’s role in keeping the journal going after the untimely death of Bob Scholte in 1987, but also how they collaborated in producing a epistemological revolution in anthropology. While most anthropologists today would associate this with Fabian’s contribution to the “literary turn” in anthropology by his more famous Time and the Other (1983) I argue that the build-up to this book shows a currently neglected but far more fundamental and visionary conception of critique that centered on an epistemological critique arising from fieldwork praxis.

extra.summary: Abdelmalek Sayad’s sociology of migration can be interpreted as an eminent form of reflexive political sociology and has more than one connection with Bourdieu’s conception of the state as state thought and the sociological-political approach outlined by the French sociologist. Firstly, by placing migrants as the unthought limit of the state, Sayad questions and challenges the classifications of state thought that present it as a homogeneous reality almost ontologically linked to the nation. On the other hand, it will be shown how the restructuring of national political fields around the national/non-national opposition, already noted by Bourdieu in the 1990s, reintroduces the theme of reformulation, in contrast to the current trend, of a radical-democratic approach. Finally, the latter should be able to deconstruct the non-essential link between state and nation from a juridical point of view (as Hans Kelsen pointed out) and thus render the discriminatory prerogatives imprinted in traditional national sovereignty unfounded.

items.title: Reforming Citizenship, Remaking the People: Nationality Law and Boundary‐Making in Contemporary Nationhood

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This article examines contemporary citizenship reforms as institutional mechanisms through which states remake the boundaries of the people. Nationalism studies have long analysed the symbolic construction of nations, while citizenship studies have explored status, rights, migration and inclusion. Yet nationality laws remain under‐theorised as legal‐political technologies of people‐making. Drawing on a qualitative, comparative and legal‐institutional approach, the article analyses four empirical blocks: the United States, Germany, Finland and Benin‐Ghana. It argues that citizenship reforms and disputes cannot be understood simply as movements towards openness or closure. Rather, they operate through four strategies of boundary‐making: restriction, liberalisation, selective integration and diasporic reconnection. Internal re‐hierarchisation is treated as a transversal dimension. The article contributes to nationalism and citizenship studies by showing how citizenship law participates in the legal, political and symbolic production of the people.

items.title: From Gastfreundschaft to Überfremdung : National Identity and the Origins of Right‐Wing Migration Politics in West Germany, 1973–1983

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This article contributes a historical perspective to scholarship on migration and right‐wing politics in Germany. By examining legal texts, party programmes and parliamentary debates, it traces how West German national identity discourses shaped immigration and foreigner policies between the guest worker recruitment stop in 1973 and the federal elections of 1983. In this crucial but oft‐neglected period, political parties renegotiated national membership criteria amid economic crisis and an emerging multicultural society. Ethnocentric conceptions of German identity by influential right‐wing politicians entrenched an understanding of immigration as a national security threat. After the so‐called refugee crisis of 2015, the far‐right Alternative für Deutschland ( AfD ) mobilised these ideals of ethnic homogeneity in narratives about eroding German sovereignty and citizenship since the guest worker era. The article highlights the importance of analysing such historical constructions and political continuities of the ‘foreigner problem’ to make sense of resurging far‐right politics across Europe today.

items.title: The price of visibility? Asian American representation and aesthetic exclusion

extra.summary: Asian American visibility has increased dramatically in recent decades, yet material violence and systemic exclusion persist alongside—and perhaps because of—this representational ‘progress’. This article theorises this paradox through a critical dialogue among three recent monographs: Esther Kim Lee’s Made-Up Asians (2022), David C. Oh’s Whitewashing the Movies (2021), and Corinne Mitsuye Sugino’s Making the Human (2024). Collectively, they reveal what I term ‘aesthetic exclusion’: the systematic monopolisation of narrative subjectivity, visual focus, and affective structures that together predetermine who is seen, erased, or mourned. Aesthetic exclusion operates at three levels—the material technology of yellowface makeup, the narrative grammar of whitewashing, and the ontological anchoring of racial allegory—constituting a ‘cognitive infrastructure’ of racial governance that persists beyond the repeal of legal exclusion. Yet the three books are not complementary: Sugino’s ontological critique fundamentally challenges Lee and Oh’s methodological premise that a ‘real Asian’ or a ‘stolen story’ exists to be restored. Taking this unresolved tension as its central thread, the article argues that representation is not a reflection of inequality but its cognitive precondition. items.title: The politics of naming and un-naming: nationalism and colonised Adibashi in Bangladesh

extra.summary: In postcolonial South Asia, Bangladesh continues to define its national identity in ways that reproduce colonial exclusions. Despite the presence of more than fifty-four Adibashi groups, state authorities continue to contest their Indigenous status and deny them constitutional recognition as Indigenous peoples. This article examines how naming practices employed by Bengali political elites contribute to the marginalisation of Indigenous communities in Bangladesh. The state adopts a homogenising model of nationalism centred on a majority identity, which denies Indigeneity and undermines Adibashi claims to land, rights, and recognition. The article argues that nationalist politics shapes naming practices and uses them as mechanisms of assimilation and exclusion. It first situates Indigeneity within international and national debates and then demonstrates that, although marginalisation is not the sole defining feature of Indigeneity, it remains a central dimension of Indigenous experience in Bangladesh and reflects the persistence of colonial forms of domination within nationalist projects.

items.title: Epistemic injustice and the Meitei revivalist movement in Manipur, India

extra.summary: Extant scholarship has largely overlooked the epistemic dimensions of the Meiteis’ religious transformation from Sanamahism to Hinduism and the subsequent emergence of Meitei revivalism. In this article, we argue that we can understand both developments better through Miranda Fricker’s framework of epistemic injustice. Fricker conceptualizes epistemic injustice as a form of existential injustice that compromises an individual’s or group’s ‘capacity as a knower’ and undermines their ability to produce knowledge. We use a multi-modal qualitative method that combines initial autoethnographic insights with triangulated secondary sources to argue that the religious transformation of Manipur inflicted epistemic injuries in the form of testimonial injustice and a deeper hermeneutical injury. Finally, we position Meitei revivalism as a consequent project of epistemic recovery, examine its internal challenges, and consider its future in light of Manipur’s extant politics.

items.title: ‘Smart court’ and digital judicialism in China
items.affiliation: Hangzhou City University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University

extra.summary: How has digital technology been applied to the operation of courts and dispute resolution in authoritarian regimes? Drawing on ethnographic research on the construction of the ‘smart court’ in China, this article explores the impact of digital technology on the judicial system and dispute resolution through the prototypical cases of the ‘shared court’ and the ‘One Network of Courts Nationwide’, which operate, respectively, outside and inside the courts. The article reveals that, unlike in democratic countries, where digital technology is used in a relatively more conservative and limited way, digital technology has been used by the Chinese Communist Party to strengthen state control, monitor society, and maintain political stability, thus giving rise to digital judicialism. The study of digital judicialism shows that while digital technology has certainly improved the efficiency of social dispute resolution to some extent, it has been reduced to a toolkit for the government to recentralize political power and guard against political risks. The findings compel researchers to reassess the role of digital technology in facilitating the resolution of disputes because it can undermine judicial independence and the development of the rule of law under authoritarianism.

items.title: Chasing Shadows: Gender, Tourism, and Everyday Corruption in Vietnam’s Northern Borderlands

extra.summary: This article examines corruption in Vietnam’s northern borderlands as transparency reforms reshape ethnic minority livelihoods in tourism and state modernization. Drawing on multi-sited feminist ethnography (2017–2024) in Lào Cai province and Sa Pa, findings reveal corruption as an intersectional, gendered institution—practices through which access is negotiated under shifting rules, discretionary enforcement, and unequal legitimacy. Clean tourism and anti-corruption campaigns can curb visible bribery yet also multiply licenses, inspections, paperwork, and language tests that heighten surveillance for those least able to comply, especially ethnic minority women. Women trekking guides, vendors, and homestay operators shoulder navigation as carework, using calibrated gifts, envelopes, detours, and relational labor to prevent delays, fines, humiliation, or livelihood restrictions. Some call this “our clean”: a local ethics of integrity and harm reduction that protects households and community standing. The article reframes anti-corruption as distributive governance and advances a feminist ethics of transparency attentive to uneven development and local agency.

items.title: ‘Dark, buried, and very Indian’: Indigenous urban inhabitation and fluvial epistemic alternatives

extra.summary: In Latin America, urbanization is deeply linked to the dispossession of Indigenous people, and to processes of racialization that constructed the city as ‘white’ in antithesis to their territories and forms of life. Yet, the majority of Indigenous people now live in urban areas. In a context of racial inequalities and epistemic violence, how are Indigenous practices of urban inhabitation produced and given meaning? How is Indigenous knowledge shaped by the urban, and how does this shape the urban in turn?. To answer these questions, the article focuses on the Mapocho river running through Santiago, Chile. A key element of Indigenous geographies, the river is at the same time the border-line that shapes the city into segregated areas—with class and race historically defining this exclusionary urbanism. Moving from the collaborative research project MapsUrbe (2017-2021), the article addresses the relational engagement with this river in order to rethink urban inhabitation as multiple, frictional, and creative, marked by loss and dispossession as well as endurance. Centered on Mapuche knowledge making and territorial imagination, the paper takes seriously fluvial epistemics to reframe urban inhabitation as the entanglement of acts of traversing, subterranean streams and silent flowing, and sudden overflooding.

This traditional house not only reflects the identity and honor of the local indigenous community but also functions as a center of cultural activities and traditional education. This study aims to examine the symbolic meanings, social functions, and preservation strategies of Lamban Gedung Kuning amid the wave of modernization. The research was conducted using a descriptive qualitative method through data collection in the form of literature review, direct observation, and in-depth interviews with traditional leaders and cultural managers. The findings indicate that Lamban Gedung Kuning plays a vital role as a residence, a center for preserving traditional values, and a medium for character education based on local culture. The preservation efforts involve active community participation, implementation of traditional rituals and ceremonies, documentation of cultural heritage objects, and education for younger generations. This study emphasizes that preserving Lamban Gedung Kuning is a crucial effort to safeguard the cultural identity of the Lampung people so that it remains sustainable and relevant in facing contemporary challenges.

items.title: Can Intangible Cultural Heritage Resources Stimulate Regional Entrepreneurial Activity?—Empirical Evidence from the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region
items.affiliation: Nanning University; Fujian Normal University; Universiti Putra Malaysia; Northern University of Malaysia

extra.summary: In line with the world’s goals of sustainable development, cultural resources are now being used to promote both cultural inheritance and regional economic revitalisation. This paper studies whether intangible cultural heritage (ICH) resources can promote regional entrepreneurial activity by analyzing panel data from 14 prefecture-level cities in the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, China, from 2007 to 2023. The empirical results indicate that ICH resources significantly promote entrepreneurial activity in Guangxi; specifically, both the stock of ICH projects and the stock of inheritors show significantly positive effects, and the findings remain robust after a series of tests. The results suggest that ICH can be used to carry cultural values and serve as a resource for place-based development that supports entrepreneurship through heritage commercialisation, cultural consumption and local industrial integration. This study incorporates ICH into the regional entrepreneurship analysis framework, providing new empirical evidence for the economic value of cultural heritage and its role in innovation-driven development.

items.title: Borderland extraterritoriality: The Yunnan-Burma frontier meetings (1902–1949)
items.affiliation: East China University of Political Science and Law

extra.summary: Abstract Britain exercised a distinctive form of extraterritorial jurisdiction around the Yunnan-Burma border before 1949. In 1902, Chinese and British officials established a joint trial system under the 1902 Manai Agreement. From then on, Chinese, British, and Burmese officials convened temporary frontier meetings each winter in border areas, including in Manai, Nawngma, and Sima. These meetings adjudicated disputes involving theft, injuries, and trans-frontier cultivation pursuant to tribal customary law. The frontier meetings normally issued four distinct types of judgments and awarded a uniform remedy in the form of damages. This system served the practical needs of border tribes by delivering swift justice to prevent blood feuds and maintain law and order. These meetings developed a case law for resolving borderland cases that diverged from the national laws of both China and Britain. This system was jointly administered by Chinese, British, and Burmese officials under ostensibly reciprocal terms, though Britain’s exercise of extraterritorial jurisdiction in China ultimately placed a heavier burden on the Chinese side. The joint trial system came to an end after Burma officially gained independence in 1948. British extraterritorial jurisdiction in China was not absolute but operated through distinct jurisdictional systems in the interior and in the borderlands.

items.title: Personalised immersion, community engagement, and place identity in China rural heritage tourism

extra.summary: The rapid tourismification of intangible cultural heritage (ICH) performance in rural China has transformed village spaces into immersive cultural landscapes, yet its temporal effects on residents’ place identity remain poorly understood. Drawing on place identity theory and community-based engagement scholarship, this study examines how residents’ perceptions of immersive heritage tourism evolve over time and influence place belonging, cultural pride, and community cohesion. A three-wave longitudinal survey was conducted across rural ICH performance destinations in Yunnan and Guizhou, China (baseline N = 420; analytical N = 378). Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling was used to separate within-person temporal fluctuations from between-person stable differences. Results reveal a dual-edged process. At the between-person level, sustained community engagement mediates a positive association between immersive heritage tourism and place identity. At the within-person level, intensified tourismification predicts erosion of perceived cultural authenticity, which is associated with weaker affective bonds to place. A positive sequential indirect effect through community engagement also accumulates across waves. These findings introduce a temporal perspective to the heritage–place identity nexus and inform more community-sensitive immersive tourism development.

extra.summary: China’s fisheries economy has long faced multiple external shocks, and enhancing its resilience is crucial to achieving sustainable development. (2) The spatial association network has always remained fully connected, with the network hierarchy degree fluctuating from 0.207 down to 0.143. items.title: Balancing Security, Development, and Ecology in Border Land Governance: An SDET Diagnostic Framework and Flexible Authorization Pathway for Advancing the SDGs in China
items.affiliation: Guangdong Police College; China People's Police University

extra.summary: Border regions are where sovereign security, economic development, and ecological protection collide most acutely. These competing demands often stall progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). However, most land governance frameworks are built for inland agricultural or urban settings. This study develops a framework that combines a Security-Development-Ecology Triad (SDET) diagnostic model with a customized Sustainability Impact Assessment (SIA) system. The framework is applied to China’s border collaborative spatial legislation. This study draws on 47 policy and legal documents (2012–2025), three internal legislative consultation minutes, and nine semi-structured interviews. The SDET model uses three measurable indicators: agenda-setting veto power, clause-weight tilt, and preset legality-review thresholds. items.affiliation: Inner Mongolia Open University; Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology; Daito Bunka University

extra.summary: Rural road plays a crucial role in improving market access, labour mobility, and public service delivery in remote regions. items.title: Donating me!? Donor fear and the difficult entanglements of clothes and persons in the transition towards a circular economy of textile reuse

extra.summary: Textile waste is estimated to reach 134 mill tons per year globally by 2030, if a circular transition is not managed. Illuminating aspects of consumer culture that prevent circular clothes reuse is thus of critical environmental importance. While management and consumer scholars have continuously investigated how reuse can be furthered through donation and circulation systems, few have looked at the reasons people may have for refusing to donate their discarded clothes for reuse. This paper investigates reasonings for refusing to donate clothes for reuse even when information, technical and political support is in place. Through qualitative analysis of detailed ethnographic accounts from users of a Danish reuse and recycling station, the article provides a nuanced understanding of the social rationales that govern deliberate decisions not to donate for reuse. Drawing on sociological and anthropological theory on the intimate entanglements of clothes and wearer, I advance the concept of donor fear to unfold how clothes become controversial if not downright (socially) dangerous to donate. Showing how clothes donation constitutes complex social risks and dangers, this study is relevant to both scholars and practitioners who want to understand and manage socio-cultural obstacles to the circular economy of textile reuse.

Second, to examine how Buddhist knowledge in Southeast Asia was transmitted, localized, and transformed through processes of adaptation, reinterpretation, and materialization. Third, to propose a framework of multidirectional knowledge circulation to explain how religious and technical forms of knowledge moved across interconnected regional networks in early Asia.
